periods.activity_title: Before We Read: Adventure, Qualities, and First Encounter

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us read (p.166): paired discussion on adventure sports and mountaineer word web.

time_bands.activity: Open with the word web on the board: 'Qualities of a mountaineer.' Invite students to call out words while the teacher records them; brief whole-class sharing follows.
Students work in pairs on the pre-reading discussion from 'Let us read' (p.166): why people undertake adventure activities, how they prepare, and which activity excites them most.

Teacher reads the full text of 'Conquering the Summit' (pp.166–169) aloud, students following in their books; pause at key moments — Arunima's injury, her vow, and her summit day — to allow quiet reflection.

periods.teacher_notes: This is students' first encounter with Arunima Sinha's story; the pre-reading word web surfaces prior knowledge about mountaineering before the text fills it in. Watch for students who conflate physical strength with the mental resilience the text emphasises — the prose_summary flags 'mental fortitude' and 'positive mindset' as the text's central themes. Students who did not contribute to the word web can be invited back once the text reading surfaces relevant qualities.
materials: Blackboard or whiteboard for word web

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.169): explain two statements about Arunima in own words.

homework.task_brief: Let us discuss (p.169): choose one remaining statement about Arunima and write a short explanation in your own words.

time_bands.activity: Briefly revisit Arunima's story — her injury, vow, training, and summit — by asking students to recall two key facts from the text before moving to discussion.

Whole-class discussion of 'Let us discuss' (p.169): take the statement 'Arunima Sinha is considered a beacon of hope and resilience' and invite students to explain it in their own words, drawing on evidence from the text.

Students work in pairs to unpack 'Bachendri Pal's guidance was crucial in Arunima's journey to the summit' (p.169); pairs share their explanations with the class and the teacher draws out the mentor-mentee relationship the text describes.

periods.teacher_notes: Having read about Arunima's journey from injury to summit, students are now asked to move from recall to interpretation. A common difficulty at this spine is students retelling events rather than explaining what a statement means — nudge them toward paraphrase and inference rather than quotation. The remaining three statements from 'Let us discuss' make a manageable homework task for reinforcement.

periods.activity_title: Thinking Deeper: Extract Analysis and Reflective Questions

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us think and reflect (p.170): extract questions on Bachendri Pal's words and summit day.

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the extract — Bachendri Pal's words to Arunima and the summit-day passage (p.170) — while students follow; then allow a brief silent re-read.

Students answer the Section I questions from 'Let us think and reflect' (p.170): the fill-in on why Bachendri Pal said Arunima had conquered the Everest within her, how Arunima might have felt, and the phrase showing physical exhaustion.

Whole-class discussion on the MCQ item about 'an overwhelming sense of achievement' (p.170) and one Section II reflective question — 'Arunima is a beacon of hope and resilience; support with evidence' — to close the reading spine on critical engagement.

periods.teacher_notes: Having discussed what Bachendri Pal's mentorship meant and what 'beacon of hope' implies, students are ready to work with the extract directly. Watch for the common confusion between Bachendri Pal's literal statement and its metaphorical meaning — the prose_summary notes her words ('you have conquered the Everest within you') as a framing device for the text's resilience theme. The remaining Section II reflective questions (autobiography title, Arunima's quote on failure) are rich but time-heavy; flag them as independent reading for interested students.

periods.activity_title: Voices on Adventure: Listening, Matching, and Role Talk

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us listen (p.173): match statements 1–8 to five speakers on adventure sports.
Let us speak (p.173): group role-play — student, parent, PE teacher, sports camp organiser.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the listening task: tell students they will hear five speakers with different views on adventure sports and must match eight statements (with three distractors) to the correct speaker.
Read the transcript (p.177) aloud twice at a measured pace; students complete the matching exercise from 'Let us listen' (p.173) individually as they listen.
Quick whole-class check of the matching answers; discuss what clues in each speaker's words helped identify their stance — parent, youth, organiser, school, or traditionalist.

Form groups of four; each student takes a role from 'Let us speak' (p.173) — school student, parent, PE teacher, or sports camp organiser — and delivers a short turn expressing their view, then the group holds a quick open exchange.

periods.teacher_notes: The five speakers in the listening transcript represent distinct stances — parental concern, youthful enthusiasm, professional safety, institutional caution, and traditional sport preference — and students often conflate speakers (ii) and (iii) because both are broadly positive about adventure. Alert students to listen for the specific focus of each speaker before they attempt the match. For the speaking role-play, gently ensure quieter students take speaking turns; the NCF pedagogy note on individual differences in classroom participation is relevant here.
materials: Listening transcript (p.177) — teacher copy for reading aloud

periods.activity_title: Words, Word Forms, and Articles in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.171): match five underlined phrases to their meanings.
Let us learn (p.171): complete the word-form table for determination, relief, inspire, resistance, success.

homework.task_brief: Let us learn (p.172): fill in blanks with a, an, the, or x in the adventure-trip passage.

time_bands.activity: Students read sentences (i)–(v) from 'Let us learn' (p.171) and match each underlined phrase — such as 'mental fortitude' and 'beacon of hope' — to the meaning from the box; pairs compare answers before a quick whole-class check.

Introduce the word-form table (p.171): teacher models the first row (determination / determined / determine / determinedly) and explains noun-adjective-verb-adverb relationships; students complete the remaining rows for relief, inspire, resistance, and success.

Teacher introduces the article grammar point (p.172) — indefinite 'a'/'an' versus definite 'the', and the zero-article — using two or three sentences from the text as anchors; students note the rule before the homework is set.

periods.teacher_notes: Having encountered phrases like 'mental fortitude' and 'beacon of hope' in the reading spine, students now anchor them formally through matching and word-building. A frequent error in the word-form table is treating 'inspiring' as only an adjective and missing 'inspire' as the verb stem — draw attention to how the column header says 'Verb (present)' and invite students to check their answers by forming a sentence. The article-correction exercise (p.172) and the longer fill-in passage are substantial; both are better placed as independent practice rather than rushed in class.

periods.activity_title: Articles in Action: Correction and Application

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us learn (p.172): correct article errors in six sentences about travel and mountains.

time_bands.activity: Quick oral recap of article rules introduced in the previous vocabulary unit — 'a' vs 'an', definite 'the', and zero article — using two student-generated examples from the class.

Students work individually on the article-correction exercise from 'Let us learn' (p.172): six sentences containing deliberate article errors (e.g., 'a hour', 'an uniform', 'a second highest peak'); teacher circulates.

Whole-class correction: take each sentence in turn, ask a student to identify the error and explain why the correction works; close by having students write two original sentences using 'the' correctly with a proper noun, modelled on the Ganga example.

periods.teacher_notes: Having introduced article rules through the text, this unit moves students to applying those rules in error correction. The most persistent errors are with proper nouns ('A Ganga' and 'A North Star') where students may not recognise that unique referents take 'the'; use the text's own mention of 'the Nehru Institute of Mountaineering' as a familiar anchor. The longer fill-in passage (fifteen blanks, p.172) was assigned for home practice; if students bring it with questions, address individual doubts briefly at the start.

periods.activity_title: Formal Letter Writing and Adventures Beyond the Text

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Let us write (p.174–175): study sample letter components, then draft formal letter to Principal requesting a hill-station excursion.
Let us explore (p.175): research five adventure sports in India and complete the information table.

time_bands.activity: Teacher displays the sample formal letter from 'Let us write' (p.174) and walks through each component — sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation, body paragraphs, complimentary close, signature — students label their own copy.

Students independently draft a formal letter to the Principal requesting a Grade 7 hill-station excursion (p.175); teacher circulates, prompting correct use of format components and reminding students to include a statement of request and an expression of interest.

Introduce the beyond-text adventure-sports research table from 'Let us explore' (p.175) — name, area, preferred season, equipment; students begin filling in what they already know for snow skiing and trekking, and the remainder becomes a library or home research task.

periods.teacher_notes: Having studied the formal letter's components through the sample, students apply the format immediately in their own writing — keeping study and production in the same unit prevents format knowledge from going cold. The most common writing error is omitting the subject line or writing an informal salutation; keep the sample visible on the board or projector throughout the drafting phase. The adventure-sports research table is well-suited as a partial in-class start followed by independent completion, as it requires access to reference material that may not be immediately available.
materials: Reference materials or textbooks for adventure sports table (if available)

periods.activity_title: Whole-Chapter Synthesis: Resilience, Language, and Adventure

time_bands.activity: Whole-class discussion: what does Bachendri Pal's phrase 'you have conquered the Everest within you' reveal about the difference between physical achievement and mental resilience? Students draw on Arunima's story to justify their answers.

Quick-review round: teacher reads three short statements aloud (one from the listening transcript, one about a mountaineer quality, one an article-use scenario) and students respond orally — connecting listening, vocabulary, and grammar knowledge built across the chapter.

Students write a short paragraph (8–10 sentences) responding to Arunima's message 'Never give up and work hard' — applying formal register, correct articles, and at least two vocabulary items from the chapter (e.g., 'mental fortitude', 'beacon of hope', 'life-altering event').

Students compare Arunima Sinha's mountaineering achievement with one other adventure sport from 'Let us explore' — briefly noting what qualities, training, and equipment each demands; two or three students share their comparisons aloud to close the chapter.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit draws together Arunima's story of resilience with the language and adventure themes built across the chapter — students connect the reading, vocabulary, grammar, and beyond-text learning. Where students struggle to use 'mental fortitude' or 'beacon of hope' in their paragraph, prompt them to recall what each phrase meant when they matched it against its definition. The comparison between Arunima's Everest climb and another adventure sport is deliberately open — it values the quality of reasoning over factual completeness.

items.source_lo: Student reads and interprets an informational biography by identifying stated facts, inferring character motivation, and evaluating thematic claims using textual evidence.
items.source_context: Arunima Sinha's injury, vow, Everest training, summit achievement, resilience, and Bachendri Pal's mentorship.
items.item_stem: Read the following statements about Arunima Sinha and her journey to the summit of Mount Everest. Decide whether each statement is true or false.

options.text: Arunima completed her mountaineering training at the Nehru Institute of Mountaineering in Rishikesh.
Arunima reached the summit of Mount Everest after 40 days of climbing.
Arunima Sinha was a national-level volleyball player before she lost her leg.
Bachendri Pal, the first Indian woman to summit Everest, mentored Arunima during her preparation.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. True — the text states she was a national-level volleyball player from Ambedkar Nagar. 2. False — the institute is in Uttarkashi, not Rishikesh. 3. True — Bachendri Pal, the first Indian woman to summit Everest, mentored Arunima. 4. False — the text states it took 52 exhausting days to reach the summit.

items.source_lo: Student reads and interprets an informational biography by identifying stated facts, inferring character motivation, and evaluating thematic claims using textual evidence.
items.source_context: Arunima Sinha's injury, vow, Everest training, summit achievement, resilience, and Bachendri Pal's mentorship.
items.item_stem: Bachendri Pal told Arunima, 'You have conquered the Everest within you.' Using evidence from the text about Arunima's response to her injury and her actions during the eighteen months of training, explain what this statement reveals about the kind of strength Arunima demonstrated. Do you think her achievement goes beyond physical endurance? Give reasons for your answer.

expected_elements: Refers to Arunima's vow in hospital despite devastating trauma.
Links 'inner Everest' to mental fortitude or positive mindset.
Cites specific training effort — eighteen months, mountaineering course.
Offers a reasoned view on whether achievement exceeds physical endurance.

items.source_context: Five speakers on adventure sports — parental concern, youthful enthusiasm, organiser safety, school caution, and traditional sport preference.
items.item_stem: Speaker (iii) and Speaker (iv) both mention safety in the context of adventure sports, but their reasons for doing so are different. After listening to the transcript, explain in two or three sentences what makes their approaches to safety distinct from each other.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: Speaker (iii) is an adventure camp organiser who actively manages safety through regular equipment checks, thorough training, and professional supervision in order to provide an exciting experience. Speaker (iv) represents a school that avoids risk altogether by restricting activities to basic, manageable sports and emphasising caution as a guiding principle — the difference is between professionally managed risk and institutional avoidance of risk.

expected_elements: States a clear position favouring physical education in school.

items.item_stem: Inspired by Arunima Sinha's spirit of adventure, you want your school to organise an outdoor trekking camp in a nearby hilly area. items.item_stem:
The passage below is about Arunima Sinha's achievement. Fill in each blank with 'a', 'an', 'the', or 'x' (where no article is needed). Write your answer above each blank number.

Arunima Sinha is (1) _______ inspiring mountaineer from Ambedkar Nagar in Uttar Pradesh. After surviving (2) _______ life-altering accident on (3) _______ moving train, she made (4) _______ vow to climb (5) _______ Mount Everest. She trained at (6) _______ Nehru Institute of Mountaineering and received guidance from Bachendri Pal, (7) _______ first Indian woman to summit Everest. On reaching (8) _______ summit, Arunima displayed (9) _______ Indian flag — (10) _______ moment of extraordinary courage and determination.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. an; 2. a; 3. a; 4. a; 5. x (Mount Everest as a proper name does not take an article in standard usage); 6. the; 7. the; 8. the; 9. the; 10. a

items.item_stem: Using what you know or have researched, write a short paragraph (5–7 sentences) describing ONE adventure sport practised in India. Include: the name of the sport, the region of India where it is popular, the best time of year to practise it, and one key piece of equipment needed. Explain briefly why you think this sport appeals to young people.

expected_elements: Names a specific adventure sport and its Indian region.
States the preferred season with a brief reason.
Identifies at least one item of equipment accurately.
Offers a reason why the sport appeals to young people.

items.source_context: Adventure sports in India — snow skiing, trekking, camping, river rafting, scuba diving — area, season, and equipment.
items.item_stem: Prepare a fact sheet for ONE Indian mountaineer of your choice (other than Arunima Sinha). Your fact sheet must cover: full name and place of birth, the mountain or summit they are most famous for, one award or honour they received, and the training or preparation that helped them succeed. Use the structure of an information booklet page — a heading, subheadings, and brief notes under each.

expected_elements: Fact sheet has a clear heading and at least three subheadings.
Includes accurate name, birthplace, and notable achievement.
Names one award or honour with a brief context.
Describes training or preparation in at least two points.
